citacoes.trecho: Through this methodology, we enhanced the architecture and structure of the evolving agentic framework for code generation, achieving a notable 98% accuracy in solving challenging coding tasks via specified workflows.
In our AI agent implementation, we crafted precise prompts tailored to each tool, ensuring the models perform as intended.
We implemented a structured iterative workflow agent (see Fig. 2), which provides process control and maintains shared state across tools throughout the entire generation flow.
A retry mechanism was also incorporated, allowing to configure code - generation attempts (a state parameter) to effectively manage unsuccessful outputs.
Analyzer: This tool verifies if a task is a coding - related one. If it is, it directs the task to the Developer; if not, it responds with a generic answer.
Developer: Responsible for designing and implementing Python code to solve the task. It also generates test cases and code to execute them. When all tests pass, the tool outputs “All tests passed.”
Evaluator: Acts as a code reviewer, validating the code, making necessary corrections, and adding comments for clarity.

Executor (Tester): Runs the code and checks for the presence of the phrase “All tests passed” in the output. If successful, it returns the result; otherwise, it sends the task back to the Developer with detected errors.
Using ensemble models with distinct roles - where the critic/validator is a separate model - proves to be an intuitive and effective approach for achieving optimal results.
This indicates that the validation model not only corrects the code but also enriches it with detailed comments, as specified in the prompt instructions.
Without proper control and reliability mechanisms, agents can exhibit unpredictable behavior, leading to high operational costs, potential security risks, and performance degradation.
Cost Control: Generative models are invoked by agents without transparency, making it difficult to track the number of calls per execution and manage associated costs.

Prompt Control: Many agent libraries conceal the actual prompts passed to LLMs, relying on complex, often opaque prompts (Fig. 1), and making decisions based on tool function comments and argument types in ReAct agents.
By design, they always generate a response, and, notably, an LLM can often produce different outputs for the same prompt due to inherent variability.
One challenge, however, is hallucination - when the model generates erroneous information that may not align with the prompt or its training data.
Testers may encounter a range of potential errors when running these scripts, and it’s essential for our agent to handle and log these issues effectively.
Our validation tool acts much like a code reviewer in a traditional SDLC, addressing a substantial portion of errors before execution.

It is beneficial if agents can work effectively for specific use cases; however, in our experience, such applications often make too many autonomous decisions, leading to frequent errors and incorrect outcomes.
React agents often suffer from inconsistent or missing state management, which can lead to unpredictable behavior and errors when state isn’t properly passed or updated across tools.
While the 4 - bit quantization of DeepSeek - Coder - V2 offers significant advantages in terms of reduced memory and power requirements, it also poses challenges in maintaining model accuracy.
This paper presents an analysis of the quantization’s impact on model fidelity and discusses potential mitigation strategies, including hybrid quantization techniques, to optimize performance.
Each LLM call is routed through AWS Bedrock Guardrails, which filters out inappropriate or offensive content.
To ensure robust monitoring and observability, we log every tool's state, utilizing AWS CloudWatch for real - time logs and alerts.
All models are from reliable and trustworthy vendors (Meta, Anthropic, AWS, Depseek - AI and Mistral), costing less than $1 per one million tokens, and MMLU benchmark over 70.

citacoes.trecho: Table II demonstrates the results for claude - 3 - haiku.
We were able to achieve very good results for solving complex development tasks from LeetCode with LLM agents with success rate of up to 98 percent for Mata’s llama3 - 2 - 11b - instruct model.
For example, claude - 3 - haiku (Table II) produces 85% accuracy after first iteration, while llama3 - 2 - 11b - instruct – only 73%.
It is ironical and impressive that the cheapest model we have chosen gives us the best results.
